timeline.name: WebCrawler
timeline.significance: Among the first crawler-based engines to search the full text of web pages.

timeline.name: Lycos
timeline.significance: Launched from work at Carnegie Mellon University and became a major commercial endeavor.

timeline.name: Yahoo! Search
timeline.significance: Search was added to Yahoo!'s human-curated directory.

timeline.name: RankDex
timeline.significance: Used hyperlinks to assess website quality.

timeline.name: Netscape search distribution deal
timeline.significance: Netscape rotated five major search providers on its search page under commercial agreements.

timeline.name: Google Search and PageRank
timeline.significance: Google launched and later rose to prominence through ranking and interface choices.

timeline.name: MSN Search
timeline.significance: Initially relied on third-party results before Microsoft moved toward its own search technology.

timeline.name: Baidu
timeline.significance: Launched using technology associated with Robin Li's work.

timeline.name: Google becomes dominant
timeline.significance: The article attributes this to ranking quality, link analysis, and a minimalist interface.

timeline.name: Yahoo! search technology consolidation
timeline.significance: Yahoo! acquired Inktomi in 2002 and Overture-owned search assets in 2003, then launched its own technology in 2004.

timeline.name: Microsoft transitions to its own search technology
timeline.significance: Microsoft moved toward its own crawler and search infrastructure.

timeline.name: Bing launches
timeline.significance: Microsoft rebranded Live Search as Bing.

timeline.name: Yahoo!-Microsoft search agreement finalized
timeline.significance: Yahoo! Search was to be powered by Bing technology.

timeline.name: YaCy
timeline.significance: A peer-to-peer search engine listed in the article's timeline.

timeline.name: Qwant, Swisscows, Kagi and others appear in timeline
timeline.significance: The article's timeline records continuing diversity in search providers.

timeline.name: Brave Search and You.com
timeline.significance: Newer search services appear in the article's chronology.

timeline.name: Perplexity
timeline.significance: The article lists Perplexity as an AI-era search product.

timeline.name: AI-powered search integration
timeline.significance: Search increasingly combines indexing with language models for conversational answers, summaries, and contextual recommendations.

early_search_system_details.name: Archie
early_search_system_details.details: Downloaded public anonymous FTP directory listings and indexed filenames, not the contents of the files.

early_search_system_details.name: Veronica
early_search_system_details.details: Keyword search over Gopher menu titles.

early_search_system_details.name: Jughead
early_search_system_details.details: Retrieved menu information from specific Gopher servers.

early_search_system_details.name: W3Catalog
early_search_system_details.details: Standardized mirrored pages of manually maintained web resource catalogs.

early_search_system_details.name: World Wide Web Wanderer
early_search_system_details.details: Captured URLs; the article notes that URLs alone often did not provide descriptive information useful for searchers.

early_search_system_details.name: ALIWEB
early_search_system_details.details: Depended on webmasters to submit index files in a specified format.

early_search_system_details.name: JumpStation
early_search_system_details.details: Combined a crawler, index, and query interface but initially had limited fields available for indexing.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Detect modification or substitution of downloaded content.

fields.label: Steps
value: Obtain the expected digest from an authenticated/trusted source.
Compute the digest of the received file with a suitable modern algorithm.
Compare values using the correct algorithm and encoding.
If a mismatch occurs, reject or investigate the file; if it matches, interpret the result only within the trust model.

fields.label: Caveats
value: A digest posted beside a file on the same unauthenticated channel may be replaced together with the file.
A matching hash does not prove that software is benign or that the publisher is trustworthy.
